extracted.intended_audience: administrative-law scholars, regulators, judges, and practitioners concerned with self-regulatory organizations (SROs) and constitutional/administrative limits
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate legal and administrative criteria governing self-regulatory organizations (SROs), including private nondelegation concerns, state-action tests, common-law preemption, and agency oversight (with a close look at SEC–FINRA procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private nondelegation doctrine concerns: arbitrariness and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The private nondelegation doctrine is concerned with both arbitrariness and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion underlies cases like Carter Coal and Amtrak II: delegations to private entities are suspect because they risk unfair (arbitrary) decisionmaking and diminish government accountability. See Froomkin citation re: accountability rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability rationale for restricting private lawmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: If a private actor can make law but is not subject to the structural protections of the Constitution, the constitutional accountability of the actor is simply nonexistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain why delegations to self-interested private actors (who are not part of constitutional scheme) raise constitutional concerns; ties to private nondelegation doctrine and due process analyses in Amtrak II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalistic 'oversight' on–off test for private delegations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court’s approach often asks only whether the privatization at issue is subject to formal oversight by a federal agency (an on–off approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sunshine Anthracite (industry proposals subordinate to Commission surveillance) and Currin (conditioning regulation on a growers’ vote where Secretary already chose content). This test is criticized for being superficial and not probing the sufficiency or substance of oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: No private imposition of majority over minority
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegation should not amount to a private imposition of the majority over the minority (a concern drawn from Currin and Carter Coal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplements the oversight inquiry by asking whether privatization effectively allows a private majority to impose policy on a disfavored minority, but historically has not been a meaningful part of analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency oversight must be substantive, not merely formal
rubrics_metrics.description: Private involvement is permissible provided that involvement is subject to agency oversight and approval—but oversight inquiry often fails to examine whether oversight is sufficient to guard against arbitrariness or promote accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although statutory schemes often require oversight, the form and sufficiency of oversight (e.g., ability to overrule or meaningfully supervise) matters for accountability but is frequently glossed over in courts’ analyses (Amtrak II considered degree of oversight more closely).

rubrics_metrics.name: State-action 'fairly attributable' test
rubrics_metrics.description: Private actors’ activities may be constrained by the Constitution if their actions are 'fairly attributable' to the government (i.e., are state action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical source: Lugar; Lebron (government-created corporations may be state actors for some purposes). The inquiry is fact-specific and requires showing a sufficient nexus to government action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicating state action: government creation, coercive power, significant encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts look for indicia such as whether the government created or controls the private entity, whether the government exercised coercive power, or whether there was significant encouragement that makes private action fairly attributable to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desiderio held SEC approval of a clause was insufficient without coercive power/significant encouragement. Hypothetical variations (e.g., SEC authority to modify a clause, or regulations requiring certain clauses) would change analysis but courts have not fully explored them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural due process requires functional inquiry into actual procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural due process reading must grapple with the doctrine’s applicability and the actual procedures at issue (i.e., whether the institutional arrangement provides the 'something more' required by due process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast formalistic readings (which may conflate doctrines) with functional due process inquiry exemplified by Londoner; courts should analyze individualized decisionmaking and substantive procedural safeguards rather than only labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO constitutional constraints occur only after oversight agency adopts the action
rubrics_metrics.description: SROs are constitutionally constrained when an impacted individual uses the Constitution as a shield and only after the oversight agency has made the action its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means individuals typically cannot bring constitutional claims directly against SROs pre-enforcement; constitutional protection functions as a defensive tool (shield) after agency adoption rather than as an affirmative protective tool (sword).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law claims against SROs are preempted when action is pursuant to federal statutory scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: When SROs act pursuant to a carefully crafted federal statutory scheme, common-law claims that conflict with that scheme are preempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better characterized as preemption rather than governmental immunity (In re Series 7). The organic SRO statute typically provides the exclusive means of challenging SRO actions; savings clauses in statutes can preserve common-law liability where desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO governance composition requirement (FINRA example)
rubrics_metrics.description: FINRA’s governing board must fairly represent members and include outsiders (persons representative of issuers and investors and not associated with a member, broker, or dealer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory reference: 15 U.S.C. § 78f(b)(3). Practical concern: some 'public' board members may have close industry ties, undermining independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO rulemaking process: sources, internal drafting, board authorization, notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals for new rules may come from various sources (members, staff, SEC); proposals undergo drafting and revision within the SRO, the Board may authorize notice-and-comment, and after comment FINRA staff revise or file with the SEC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FINRA rulemaking process includes internal committee drafting, possible notice-and-comment, SEC filing; FINRA also issues guidance documents (e.g., Regulatory Notices).

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC statutory review standards and timelines for SRO rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When an SRO files a rule with the SEC, the SEC must review it, conduct notice-and-comment, assess anticompetitive impacts, and within 45 days approve/disapprove or institute proceedings; the agency may not approve earlier than 30 days without good cause; if proceedings are instituted, a hearing opportunity must be provided within 180 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory citations: 15 U.S.C. § 78s(b)(1), (b)(2)(A), (b)(2)(B), (b)(2)(C). A proposed rule is deemed approved if the SEC misses deadlines unless extended for stated reasons or with SRO consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC deference practice and ability to abrogate SRO rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice the SEC almost never disapproves SRO rules and review is often deferential; when it approves a rule the Commission finalizes it with a statement of basis and purpose; the SEC can also abrogate, add to, or delete from an SRO rule following notice-and-comment under §78s(c) and APA requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques note SEC functions as a 'watchful guard' and engages in negotiations with SROs; evidence of deference appears in GAO and consultant reports and in historical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRO enforcement/adjudication procedures and appellate review path
rubrics_metrics.description: SRO enforcement proceedings begin with a Hearing Panel, with appeal to the SRO’s National Adjudicatory Council, discretionary Board review, then SEC review de novo (with authority to affirm, modify, set aside, or remand), and finally review by a federal court of appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory framework: 15 U.S.C. § 78o-3(h), §78s(d), §78s(e), §78y(a). This procedural ladder shapes where constitutional or administrative claims can be raised and when judicial review is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight-effectiveness criteria and statutory/GAO/Dodd-Frank requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Dodd-Frank mandates periodic scrutiny of SEC–SRO relationships (GAO reports every three years; SEC hiring independent consultant; SEC reporting to Congress), and GAO/consultant reports have recommended stronger oversight, centralized coordination, and improved processes to evaluate rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings include that SEC rarely disapproves rules, lacks formal processes to evaluate rule effectiveness, faces volume/complexity challenges, and lacks statutory authority to ensure cross-market consistency; recommendations include dashboards, centralized coordination, and strengthened review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design features that influence state-action and accountability outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific design choices—such as whether the oversight agency has authority to modify SRO rules, whether it exercises coercive power, or whether the agency has made the action its own—affect whether private delegation is vulnerable under state action or nondelegation principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article notes these are under-examined questions (e.g., would SEC modification authority change Desiderio?), and that small design differences across statutory schemes (SEC–FINRA, CFTC–NFA, FERC–NERC) have major implications for accountability and constitutional exposure.
